abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: Plant pathogenic fungi have evolved molecular arsenals that enable them to successfully invade their host plants and ultimately achieve colonization. These mechanisms involve multifaceted and complex processes that require spatiotemporal regulation of various genes. The cosmopolitan genus Fusarium has been recognized worldwide as an important group of plant pathogens that exhibit diverse virulence mechanisms. This review seeks a broad overview of (a) how the virulence factors and their regulatory mechanisms are specifically utilized during the early invasion process in Fusarium species, (b) the gene regulatory mechanisms that govern this process, and (c) future directions for molecular genetics in disease control by directly targeting virulence factors in plant pathogenic fungi. By integrating current knowledge of key virulence factors and intrinsic mechanisms in Fusarium–plant systems, this work aims to provide a comprehensive understanding of Fusarium-mediated pathogenesis, with particular emphasis on the early stages of infection. Finally, we outline the shared and species-specific contributions of virulence factors, integrating findings from previous studies across individual Fusarium species.

body.p: Plant pathogenic fungi have evolved diverse strategies to invade their hosts and establish disease. The invasion strategies differ according to fungal species, lifestyle, and host specificity. Some pathogens secrete an array of virulence factors—such as cell wall–degrading enzymes (CWDEs), secondary metabolites, and effectors—that facilitate penetration. In parallel, environmental cues, including chemical and physical signals from the plant surface, reprogram morphogenetic processes that lead to the formation of infection structures. Collectively, these mechanisms enable plant pathogenic fungi to coordinate molecular and morphological processes that promote efficient host infection.

The genus Fusarium comprises a diverse group of plant pathogens, including the Fusarium head blight (FHB) pathogen Fusarium graminearum and the vascular wilt pathogen F. oxysporum, both ranked among the most economically important plant pathogens (Dean et al., 2012; Summerell, 2019). Fusarium species infect a wide range of cereal crops—including wheat, barley, maize, and rice—as well as numerous horticultural crops such as tomato, melon, banana, and cotton (Bahadur, 2021). Beyond plants, some Fusarium species have also been reported to infect humans and insects (Berasategui et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2006; Zhang et al., 2020). Plant disease symptoms caused by Fusarium infections are also diverse, ranging from head and leaf blight to vascular wilt, root and stem rot, and cankers (Fig. 1). Given the diversity in host range and virulence strategies, it is essential to investigate virulence factors at the species level.

body.p: The initial infection phase is pivotal to the entire pathogenesis process, as it marks the first step in overcoming the plant’s defenses and initiating colonization. During early infection, plant pathogens undergo several shared processes accompanied by rapid genetic reprogramming. First, they detect various biotic and abiotic plant-derived signals that guide their growth toward the host (Haueisen and Stukenbrock, 2016). This sensing is largely mediated by mitogen-activated protein kinases (MAPKs), which rapidly perceive environmental cues and transmit extracellular signals to intracellular responses (Cargnello and Roux, 2011). Pathogens then differentiate specialized infection structures that enable them to breach plant cells, often in conjunction with the secretion of numerous virulence factors such as CWDEs, secondary metabolites, and effectors (Mendgen and Deising, 1993). After penetration, the pathogen invades host tissues to secure nutrients necessary for growth and reproduction (Haueisen and Stukenbrock, 2016). Transcription factors (TFs) participate in this process by acting as key mediators of cellular functions and regulating multiple pathways through transcriptional reprogramming (Guo et al., 2014; Weidemüller et al., 2021). In addition, carbon metabolic enzymes play an essential role in nutrient acquisition and energy production (Goulet and Saville, 2017). Therefore, the regulatory mechanisms in plant pathogenic fungi are critical for successfully initiating host invasion.

In this review, we focus on and compare key virulence factors involved in the early invasion phase of plant pathogenic Fusarium species, highlighting those that contribute to the early infection process at the single-gene level. Specifically, we revisit virulence-associated genes in two major categories: (1) host-targeting molecular virulence factors, including CWDEs, secondary metabolites, and effectors, and (2) intrinsic mechanisms that operate within the fungal pathogen during early invasion. This review aims to provide a comprehensive understanding of the initial infection strategies of Fusarium species, emphasizing both their shared and species-specific features.

sec.title: Early Infection Structures in Fusarium Species
sec.p: Fusarium species have evolved their infection structures differently from the rice blast fungus Magnaporthe oryzae, which has a representative penetration structure, the appressorium. During the penetration phase, M. oryzae perceives a hydrophobic surface and differentiates into specialized structures, such as the melanized single-celled appressorium, which generates the mechanical force needed to breach the plant cell wall (Wilson and Talbot, 2009). However, it is generally believed that Fusarium species invade host tissues without forming an appressorium (Boenisch and Schäfer, 2011; Kikot et al., 2009). Instead, the fungus either enters the host through natural openings or penetrates the epidermal cell walls directly with short infection hyphae (Pritsch et al., 2000).

In the wheat head blight fungus F. graminearum, epiphytically grown hyphae on the plant surface invade through stomata, damaged tissue, or directly via runner hyphae, which can differentiate into infection cushions (Boenisch and Schäfer, 2011; Mentges et al., 2020). Such multicellular infection cushion structures can establish several penetration sites, which facilitate fungal invasion of the host plant. Similar structures were also observed on the stomatal surface of maize leaves infected by F. proliferatum (Nguyen et al., 2016). In contrast, direct penetration or the formation of a swelling at a hyphal tip originating from a single hypha was observed with F. verticillioides.

As revealed by laser capture microdissection and RNA-Seq, both runner hyphae and infection cushion upregulate numerous infection-related genes, including carbohydrate-active enzymes, putative effectors, and secondary metabolism gene clusters (Mentges et al., 2020). Runner hyphae specifically induces genes involved in aurofusarin biosynthesis, while infection cushion upregulates a broader set of virulence factors, including deoxynivalenol (DON) and fusaoctaxin A (Mentges et al., 2020). These findings suggest that F. graminearum develops specialized multicellular structures that accumulate virulence factors for effective penetration. Consistently, the G-protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) GIV1 deletion mutant was defective in infection cushion formation, a defect was restored by exogenous cAMP or by expression of a constitutively active Fst7 MEK kinase, highlighting the importance of G protein signaling in infection cushion production (Jiang et al., 2019).

In the seed-borne pathogen F. fujikuroi, hyphae colonize primarily the husk but are also detected in embryo and endosperm, where swollen-tip hyphae, infectious hyphae, and infection cushion structures are formed during rice infection (Sunani et al., 2020). By contrast, in F. oxysporum, no specialized penetration structure has been observed (Zhang et al., 2015). Instead, direct penetration occurs through branched hyphae that infect roots mainly in the meristematic zone, with penetration reduced in the elongation and root hair zones and absent in the lateral root zone (Rodríguez-Gálvez and Mendgen, 1995). Taken together, the development of infection structures reflects species-specific differentiation among Fusarium spp. Furthermore, early infection structures are spatiotemporally regulated, highlighting the genetic orchestration during the early infection stage in Fusarium spp.

sec.title: Key Genetic Factors Involved in Early Plant Penetration in Fusarium Species
Host targeting arsenal: molecules for host manipulation CWDEs
sec.p: The plant cell wall is the initial physical and defensive barrier protecting plants against pathogens. Below the cuticle, the plant cell wall includes the middle lamella, which serves as the outermost layer binding adjacent cells together (Alberts, 2002). It is a complex polysaccharide network composed predominantly of cellulose, xylan, and pectin (Guzha et al., 2022). Because the plant cell wall functions as the primary interface between host and pathogen, plant pathogens recognize the cell wall and secrete extracellular hydrolytic enzymes that disintegrate it, thereby facilitating penetration and colonization.

Fungal CWDEs are broadly classified into cellulases, xylanases, and pectinases. Among pectinases, key enzymes include exo-/endo-polygalacturonases (PGs) and pectin lyases (PLs). Because CWDEs often exhibit overlapping functions, single-gene knockouts may not fully reveal their contribution to virulence; therefore, synergistic effects among multiple polygalacturonases have been investigated (Paccanaro et al., 2017). In F. oxysporum, endo-polygalacturonases (Pg1 and Pg5) and exo-polygalacturonases (Pgx4 and Pgx6) are strongly expressed during tomato infection. While individual knockouts had little impact on virulence, the Δpg1Δpgx6 double deletion mutant displayed markedly reduced virulence, demonstrating that the combined activities of endo-polygalacturonases and exo-polygalacturonases are critical for infection (Bravo Ruiz et al., 2016). Furthermore, exo-polygalacturonases Pgx4 induces host cell necrosis, and its deletion abolishes wilt symptoms in banana caused by F. oxysporum f. sp. cubense race 4 (Dong et al., 2020).

In F. graminearum, three pectin lyases (FgPel1–3) partially contribute to virulence on wheat spikelets without affecting vegetative growth or conidiation (Cai et al., 2024). Similarly, in F. sacchari, deletion of pectin lyase-encoding genes produced significantly smaller necrotic lesions on sugarcane leaves compared to the wild type (Wang et al., 2023a). Beyond pectinases, xylanases also play important roles in virulence. F. graminearum encodes six endo-xylanases, of which XylA is indispensable for colonization in wheat and barley; notably, its deletion phenotype could not be complemented by overexpression of other xylanase genes (Tini et al., 2020). Similarly, in F. oxysporum, only one xylanase appears to play a critical role in virulence, whereas others (Xyl3 and Xyl4) are dispensable (Gómez-Gómez et al., 2002).

sec.title: Secondary metabolites
sec.p: Fusarium produces numerous secondary metabolites, including mycotoxins. Mycotoxins not only contaminate grain and threaten human and livestock health (Krska et al., 2008), but are also secreted during the early stages of invasion, directly damaging host cells and facilitating penetration.

Trichothecenes, mainly produced by F. graminearum, are well-known virulence factors in wheat floral tissues, with nivalenol (NIV) and DON being representative members of this family. DON is synthesized and secreted during plant infection and functions as a ribosome-binding translational inhibitor (Brown et al., 2004). Its biosynthesis is initiated by the TRI5 gene, which encodes trichodiene synthase, and proceeds through additional enzymes encoded within the trichothecene gene cluster (Hohn et al., 1993; McCormick et al., 2004; McCormick et al., 2006). DON biosynthesis is indispensable for virulence, as DON is crucial for cell-to-cell spread during early invasion; deletion of TRI5 restricts the fungus from traversing plasmodesmata in host tissues (Armer et al., 2024). These findings indicate that DON secretion is tightly regulated both spatially and temporally. In addition, another secondary metabolite, fusaoctaxin A, encoded by Nrps5 and Nrps9 in F. graminearum, also contributes to early invasion of wheat coleoptile (Jia et al., 2019). Deletion of the fusaoctaxin A gene cluster abolishes cell-to-cell penetration, a defect that can be restored by exogenous fusaoctaxin A.

Fusaric acid (FA) is produced by several Fusarium species, including F. oxysporum, F. verticillioides, and F. fujikuroi, and has long been recognized for its broad toxicity to both animal and plant cells (Bacon et al., 1996; Gaumann, 1957). Although the cellular basis of its toxicity remains poorly understood, one proposed mechanism involves its ability to chelate transition metals such as copper, iron, and zinc (López-Díaz et al., 2018; Ruiz et al., 2015). Fusaric acid biosynthesis is mediated by the polyketide synthase (PKS) Fub1 and was initially described as a five-gene cluster, later expanded to a 12-gene cluster (Brown et al., 2015). Functional analyses have confirmed its importance for virulence: deletion of FUB1 in F. oxysporum abolished fusaric acid production and impaired early invasion in the host plant (López-Díaz et al., 2018), while deletion of the NRPS-like carboxylic acid reductase FUB8 delayed wilt symptom development. These findings support a causal link between fusaric acid phytotoxicity, metal chelation, and early stages of virulence (Dong et al., 2025).

Fumonisins, another group of mycotoxins, are carcinogenic secondary metabolites produced by F. proliferatum, F. verticillioides, and F. fujikuroi (Gelderblom et al., 1988; Rheeder et al., 2002). Among the fumonisin A, B, C, and P series, the fumonisin B (FB1, FB2, and FB3) analogs are the most abundant, with FB1 typically detected at the highest levels (Marasas, 1996; Nelson et al., 1993). Their biosynthesis requires the polyketide synthase Fum1, with transcriptional activation by the cluster-specific regulator Fum21 (Proctor et al., 2003). Deletion of fumonisin biosynthetic genes (FUM1, FUM6, FUM8, and FUM21) in F. proliferatum completely abolished fumonisin production and pathogenicity, demonstrating their importance for fungal virulence (Sun et al., 2019). However, the precise phytotoxic role of fumonisins and their contribution to the initial stages of host invasion remain less well defined compared with DON and fusaoctaxin A.

sec.title: Effectors
sec.p: Plant pathogens deploy effector proteins to suppress host immune responses, thereby facilitating colonization and disease development (Dodds and Rathjen, 2010). Although many studies focus on identifying potential fungal Avr proteins corresponding to plant resistance (R) receptors, this review emphasizes Fusarium effectors that physiologically contribute to early infection. In Fusarium species, F. oxysporum abundantly secretes effectors during the early biotrophic stage, consistent with its predominantly apoplastic growth. Among these, the Secreted in Xylem (SIX) effectors are detected in xylem sap, with most being unique to F. oxysporum except for Six6 (Gawehns et al., 2014; Rep et al., 2004). Of the 14 characterized SIX effectors, deletion of SIX8 in F. oxysporum f. sp. cubense tropical race 4 significantly reduced disease severity (An et al., 2019). Furthermore, proteomic analyses of apoplastic fluids from tomato roots identified three early root colonization effectors that are critical for early invasion of both root and stem tissues (Redkar et al., 2022).

Because most fungal effectors are secreted cysteine-rich proteins, they can be computationally predicted using tools such as TargetP and EffectorP (Emanuelsson et al., 2000; Sperschneider et al., 2016). In F. graminearum, secretome prediction has identified several effector candidates, including Nls1 and Fg01831 (FGSG_01831), whose expression was strongly induced in infected wheat spikelets (Brown et al., 2012). Deletion of the genes significantly reduced initial infection and restricted hyphal spread within the spike (Hao et al., 2020; Hao et al., 2023). In addition, proteomic analysis of culture supernatants identified two effectors, Fg12 and Fg62, which partially contribute to virulence (Wang et al., 2023b; Yang et al., 2021). Collectively, these studies demonstrate that F. graminearum effectors play critical roles in the early stages of host invasion.

Some effectors also possess direct physiological functions by interacting with plant cell components and causing cellular damage. Typically, these function as enzymes such as proteases or hydrolases. For example, the effector protease Tpp1 is secreted during wheat infection, where it suppresses host MAPK signaling by localizing to chloroplasts, thereby weakening plant immune defenses (Darino et al., 2025). In addition, FgEc10 interacts with wheat fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase (TaFah) and promotes its degradation via the 26S proteasome pathway (Shang et al., 2025). Serine carboxypeptidases (SCPs) members of the α/β hydrolase protease family, are also implicated in virulence; deletion of FgSCP impaired the initial infection process, fungal development, and DON biosynthesis (Liu et al., 2024). Taken together, these findings highlight that Fusarium effectors not only suppress host immunity but also act directly as enzymatic proteins, both within the fungus and in host tissues, to promote penetration and disease establishment.

sec.title: Intracellular regulators: orchestrators of invasion progress
MAPK/cAMP- protein kinase A signaling pathway
sec.p: Signal transduction is critical for perceiving environmental cues and orchestrating penetration. G proteins are universal regulators of downstream MAPK and cAMP– protein kinase A pathways in eukaryotes (Li et al., 2007). In F. oxysporum, deletion of G protein subunit genes abolished pathogenicity, confirming their essential role in infection (Delgado-Jarana et al., 2005; Guo et al., 2016; Jain et al., 2002; Jain et al., 2005). In F. graminearum, more than 100 G-protein-coupled receptors have been identified, and five genes (GIV1–GIV5) are strongly induced during plant infection (Jiang et al., 2019). In particular, deletion of GIV1 disrupted infection cushion formation, a phenotype that was restored by exogenous cAMP or by expression of constitutively active Fst7 MEK kinase, suggesting that cAMP signaling is crucial for infection structure development (Hu et al., 2014).

MAPK pathways regulate diverse cellular processes through protein phosphorylation (Qi and Elion, 2005). Three MAPKs—Mgv1, Hog1, and Pmk1—are conserved in Fusarium spp. and are required for fungal development and virulence (Li et al., 2012; Pareek and Rajam, 2017; Segorbe et al., 2017). These MAPKs also show functional interplay: for example, deletion of HOG1 partially suppressed the defects of the MGV1 deletion mutant, possibly through overexpression of PMK1 in F. graminearum (Ren et al., 2019). Triple deletion of all three MAPKs caused severe growth defects, hypersensitivity to abiotic stresses, and profound impairment of plant infection (Ren et al., 2022).

Mgv1 is a central regulatory hub, and its deletion results in severe growth defects and impaired cell wall integrity in F. graminearum (Hou et al., 2002). Beyond morphogenesis, Mgv1 regulates numerous biosynthetic gene clusters (BGCs) in coordination with Tri6, thereby fine-tuning secondary metabolite production (Shostak et al., 2023). Mechanistically, Mgv1 interacts with the TF Rlm1, enabling recruitment of both the SWI/SNF (Switch/sucrose non-fermentable) and SAGA (Spt-Ada-Gcn5 acetyltransferase) chromatin remodeling complexes, which facilitate transcriptional activation of virulence-associated genes (Xu et al., 2025).

The high-osmolarity glycerol (HOG) pathway is essential for osmotic stress tolerance and also contributes to secondary metabolism, fungal development, and virulence in Fusarium species (Adám et al., 2008; Pareek and Rajam, 2017; Xia et al., 2024). In F. graminearum, Hog1 is also required for Ca2+ homeostasis: Ca2+ treatment induces Hog1 phosphorylation, and phosphorylated Hog1 is imported into the nucleus via the importin-β protein Nmd5, independently of the calcineurin pathway (Zhang et al., 2023). In F. verticillioides, Hog1 directly phosphorylates TF Crz1 to maintain Ca2+ balance (Xia et al., 2024). In F. asiaticum, Hog1 is functionally connected to the white collar complex (WCC); overexpression of HOG1 in a ΔFawc1 strain restored ROS tolerance and pathogenicity (Tang et al., 2023).

Pmk1, another core MAPK, regulates hyphal growth, conidiation, and virulence across Fusarium species (Jenczmionka et al., 2003; Urban et al., 2003; Zhang et al., 2011; Zhao et al., 2011). In F. graminearum, it also induces extracellular enzyme activities—endoglucanase, xylanolytic, and proteases—that facilitate host penetration (Jenczmionka and Schäfer, 2005). Together, MAPKs constitute an integrated signaling network that orchestrates stress responses, developmental processes, and virulence during the early stages of plant infection.

sec.title: TFs
sec.p: TFs act as key regulators that translate external and internal signals into gene expression programs (Shelest, 2008). During infection, pathogens undergo rapid transcriptional reprogramming to adapt to host environments and initiate colonization (Guo et al., 2014). In Fusarium species, transcription factor–encoding genes are predicted to constitute approximately 5–6% of the genome (Guo et al., 2014; Ma et al., 2010; Park et al., 2008). In F. graminearum, approximately 700 TFs have been identified, with systematic phenome analyses revealing that 62 are essential for virulence (Son et al., 2011b).

Several TFs participate in signal transduction pathways to sense external cues and regulate virulence-related gene expression. The Ca2+/calcineurin-responsive TF Crz1 is a key mediator of calcineurin signaling, regulating ionic homeostasis and cell wall integrity, and thereby facilitating early infection in F. graminearum (Chen et al., 2019). Other TFs act downstream of MAPK pathways. For example, the homeodomain TF Ste12, a well-characterized target of the Fus3/Kss1 MAPK, is conserved across fungi (Qi and Elion, 2005; Wong Sak Hoi and Dumas, 2010). However, its role appears to vary among Fusarium species: in F. graminearum FgSte12 regulates the secretion of CWDEs, whereas in F. oxysporum it does not, suggesting functional divergence (Gu et al., 2015; Wong Sak Hoi and Dumas, 2010). The basic-region leucine zipper (bZIP)-type TF Atf1 also functions downstream of the HOG pathway (Hagiwara et al., 2014). In F. oxysporum f. sp. cubense and F. verticillioides, FoATF1 deletion mutants show hypersensitivity to H2O2 and defects in early invasion (Qi et al., 2013; Szabó et al., 2020). In F. graminearum, constitutive expression of ATF1 partially rescued the phenotypes of HOG1 mutants (Van Nguyen et al., 2013). These findings suggest that TF-mediated signaling links environmental perception with virulence factor activation during penetration.

Other TFs control core biological processes specifically required for penetration. For instance, the Zn(II)2Cys6 zinc finger TF Art1 promotes starch hydrolysis, thereby affecting both trichothecene and fumonisin biosynthesis (Oh et al., 2016). Deletion of SWI6, a transcription cofactor involved in cell cycle and cell wall regulation, disrupts cellulose utilization and abolishes pathogenicity (Liu et al., 2013). A MADS-box TF Rlm1, acting downstream of the cell wall integrity (CWI) pathway, is likewise required for cell wall integrity and virulence in both F. graminearum and F. oxysporum (Ding et al., 2020; Yun et al., 2014).

Among Fusarium TFs, some are known to directly regulate the expression of virulence factors. Tri6 specifically controls trichothecene biosynthetic genes under nitrogen limitation and is indispensable for virulence (Nasmith et al., 2011; Seong et al., 2009). The C2H2 TF Czf1 regulates fusaric acid biosynthesis genes in F. oxysporum, influencing fusaric acid production and contributing to adhesion and invasive growth, although it is not essential for penetration (Yun et al., 2019). Sge1 in F. graminearum (Fgp1) is important for DON production, as its deletion results in reduced DON biosynthetic gene expression (Jonkers et al., 2012). Intriguingly, the F. oxysporum Sge1 cannot fully complement the F. graminearum mutant, reflecting species-specific divergence: in F. oxysporum, Sge1 ortholog instead regulates SIX effector expressions, contributing to early infection (Michielse et al., 2009; Zhao et al., 2020). Likewise, the Zn(II)2Cys6 TF Ftf1 in F. oxysporum positively regulates SIX effectors (Niño-Sánchez et al., 2016).

sec.title: Carbon metabolic enzymes
sec.p: Carbon metabolism in fungi is primarily driven by the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle and auxiliary pathways that replenish or balance its intermediates. Because genes encoding core TCA cycle enzymes are generally essential and often present in multiple copies, single-gene functional studies are challenging. Nonetheless, functional analyses have revealed specific contributions of individual enzymes to fungal virulence. For example, disruption of the malate dehydrogenase-encoding gene in F. oxysporum reduced penetration ability and delayed symptom development (Huang et al., 2023). The succinate dehydrogenase (SDH) complex also displays species- and subunit-specific functions: in F. fujikuroi, SDH subunits A, B, and D are indispensable for virulence (Fan et al., 2024), whereas in F. graminearum and F. asiaticum, virulence is specifically associated with SDH subunit C, which is also linked to resistance against SDH inhibitors (SDHIs) (Chen et al., 2024; Sun et al., 2023).

Beyond the TCA cycle, shunt pathways help maintain metabolic balance and contribute to early infection. The glyoxylate shunt, first identified as a virulence determinant in the animal pathogenic fungus Candida albicans (Lorenz and Fink, 2001), is also important in F. graminearum. Expression of malate synthase (MLS) increases rapidly during infection, and its deletion abolishes fungal development and virulence (Hao et al., 2025). Interestingly, however, isocitrate lyase (ICL1)—another key enzyme of the glyoxylate cycle—appears dispensable for virulence in F. graminearum, in contrast to its essential role in M. oryzae (Lee et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2003). The methylcitrate cycle also contributes to infection: methylisocitrate lyase (MCL1), which cleaves methylisocitrate into pyruvate and succinate, has a modest effect on its own but becomes essential when combined with deletion of ICL1 in F. graminearum (Lee et al., 2009). Pyruvate carboxylase (PYC), an anaplerotic enzyme catalyzing the conversion of pyruvate to oxaloacetate, contributes to virulence in a species-dependent manner; F. oxysporum relies more heavily on anaplerotic flux than F. graminearum to support both fungal development and early infection (Shin et al., 2024). These findings emphasize that carbon metabolism functions in a species-specific manner, and its regulation can critically shape fungal virulence.

In addition to core pathways, auxiliary metabolic enzymes underscore how central carbon metabolism directly influences virulence traits. In F. oxysporum, mutations in alcohol dehydrogenase (ADH) significantly delayed disease progression on tomato plants (Corrales Escobosa et al., 2011). In F. graminearum, the ATP citrate lyase genes (ACL1 and ACL2)—responsible for producing cytosolic acetyl-CoA—are essential for virulence, as deletion of the genes completely abolishes pathogenicity (Son et al., 2011a). Collectively, carbon pathways influence downstream processes such as energy metabolism and biosynthesis, thereby facilitating fungal pathogenesis. Moreover, because lifestyles and carbon-utilization strategies differ among species, the contributions of specific carbon-metabolic enzymes to fungal development and virulence can vary, highlighting the need for species-level genetic studies (Fig. 2).

sec.title: Translational research for disease control
sec.p: Advances in genome editing and molecular genetic tools have facilitated the identification of key virulence factors and direct application of the knowledge in agricultural practice. Targeting specific genetic process can be crucial for developing novel and efficient strategies to control plant diseases while minimizing unintended consequences for agroecosystem stability. Building on systemic insights into the early infection processes of Fusarium, several strategies—including chemical, biological, and transgenic approaches—can be applied to subvert this critical stage of pathogenesis.

Current management of Fusarium diseases relies heavily on chemical fungicides, underscoring the importance of targeting key biological components essential for early infection (Machado et al., 2017; Wegulo et al., 2015). For example, some fungicides act on MAPK pathways which function as early signaling components, while others, such as SDHIs, interfere with carbon metabolism (Bastidas et al., 2008). In addition, novel chemicals strategies—including inhibitors of CWDEs or Golgi-mediated trafficking required for effector secretion—have recently been reported, providing new avenues to suppress the early stages of infection (Juge, 2006; Toquin et al., 2009; Zhang and Xu, 2014). Integration of genomics and fungicide chemistry in future research will facilitate more targeted and sustainable management of plant pathogens.

Biological and RNA-based technologies provide sustainable alternatives for Fusarium control. Biocontrol agents such as Bacillus and Trichoderma species can suppress infection by inhibiting CWDE activity or degrading mycotoxins (Guzmán-Guzmán et al., 2025; Li et al., 2022). RNA interference (RNAi) strategies are also gaining prominence, particularly host-induced gene silencing (HIGS) and spray-induced gene silencing (SIGS). HIGS has demonstrated that silencing virulence factors required for early infection via host-produced double-stranded RNA (dsRNA)—such as PMK1 and TRI5 in F. graminearum—reduces fungal infection in wheat (Shuai et al., 2024). Importantly, SIGS represents a powerful non-transgenic approach in which exogenous dsRNA targets essential fungal genes required for early infection. Candidate genes tested for SIGS include genes encoding the MAPK Mgv1, chitin synthases, and cytochrome P450 lanosterol C-14α-demethylases (Cyp51s), as well as other essential genes (Feng et al., 2025; Kim et al., 2023; Koch et al., 2016). Because SIGS is applied at the onset of infection, it constitutes an environmentally friendly and field-deployable strategy to suppress invasion at its earliest stage.

In addition, resistance breeding guided by effector–host interactions remains a cornerstone of disease management. In tomato, transient expression of the R gene I-2 and I-3 reduces colonization by F. oxysporum (Catanzariti et al., 2015; Šimkovicová et al., 2024). Furthermore, members of the tomato TOPLESS family (TPL1 and TPL2) interact with the F. oxysporum Six8 effector; CRISPR-generated tomato mutants lacking these genes exhibited higher levels of resistance (Aalders et al., 2024). In the case of F. graminearum, the wheat transcription factor TaNfxl1 represses DON-induced defense responses, and genome-edited wheat lines effectively suppress fungal infection, indicating that TaNfxl1 plays a negative role in FHB resistance (Brauer et al., 2020). These observations suggest that CRISPR-based plant genome editing enables rapid validation of gene-targeted approaches for pathogen control. In summary, these findings underscore how dissecting early invasion mechanisms at the genetic level can inform innovative and sustainable strategies for crop protection (Fig. 3).

For pathogen control, chemical treatments and RNAi-based strategies targeting the intrinsic fungal pathways represent promising approaches to suppress early infection. In addition, transgenic plants harboring resistance receptors can effectively inhibit pathogen invasion by enhancing plant immunity. This figure was created using BioRender.

sec.title: Conclusions and Perspectives
sec.p: Fungal plant pathogens have evolved sophisticated strategies to invade their hosts and establish successful colonization. Central to the invasion process is their ability to deploy a suite of molecular weapons in a coordinated manner while minimizing energy expenditure and metabolic cost. During the initial infection phase, pathogens rapidly perceive environmental cues, reprogram transcription to fit the infection context, reorganize carbon metabolism to exploit available substrates, and secrete virulence factors in a highly coordinated manner. This review has highlighted the early-stage infection strategies in Fusarium from a genetic perspective, emphasizing both conserved and species-specific adaptations that underpin successful host invasion.

We revisited Fusarium virulence factors whose gene deletion impairs early invasion (Table 1). First, we considered the virulence factors employed by Fusarium species. Because CWDEs are often encoded in multiple copies and exhibit functional redundancy, it is challenging to assess the contribution of individual enzymes to virulence. Nevertheless, studies using multiple deletions or synergy analyses clearly indicate that CWDEs are indispensable for early penetration. Likewise, secondary metabolites and effectors show striking species-specific variation. Their presence, conservation, and contribution to virulence differ markedly among Fusarium species, underscoring the importance of species-level approaches.

sec.p: Second, we examined intrinsic regulatory mechanisms that govern the early invasion process. The signaling pathways are tightly linked to fungal development—including hyphal growth, cell wall remodeling, and secondary metabolism—and ultimately influence the initial invasion. TFs participate in early invasion through three main mechanisms: (1) coordination with upstream signal transduction pathways, (2) regulation of key biological processes required for invasion, and (3) direct regulation of virulence factor expression. Given the diverse and specialized roles of TFs, individual functional characterization remains essential for understanding the complex regulatory networks underlying infection. With respect to carbon metabolism, enzymes supporting the TCA cycle and associated shunt pathways make crucial contributions during the invasion process, highlighting the substantial energy demands at this stage.

Finally, considering that Fusarium species have evolved to infect a wide range of hosts—including plants, insects, and humans—understanding both shared and host-specific infection mechanisms is crucial (Fig. 1). For example, some F. oxysporum are pathogenic to humans, while others form symbiotic associations with insect or cause disease in plant (Berasategui et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2020). These different lifestyles suggest that Fusarium pathogenesis and symbiosis must be studied at the species level. Considering that the initial invasion process is a common feature of fungal pathogens regardless of host, comparative studies of orthologous genes across different species or hosts can provide valuable insights into virulence strategies.

In conclusion, our review highlights the key genetic mechanisms governing the early infection process in Fusarium spp. Future research should prioritize systematic and species-level characterization of virulence factors, transcriptional regulators, and metabolic pathways associated with early infection. Such knowledge will not only deepen our mechanistic understanding of Fusarium infection biology but also lay the foundation for innovative approaches to sustainable plant disease control.
